algorithm: Eight four-bit least-significant-digit passes of the original SDK unsigned 32-bit radix sort: local 512-key partition, 256-key offsets, hierarchical counter scan, uniform addition, and global reorder.
mapping: Six device kernels per digit; original per-stage launch geometry retained. Full-block Hillis-Steele scan replaces native implicit warp scan only within local sorting.

reference_audit.finding: Historical CUDA.jl substitutes high-level sort! for the native four-stage SDK radix pipeline. This is an algorithm/mapping difference, not evidence of a wrong sorting operator. Its single sort elapsed time is divided by repeat without repeating the sort, a separate historical S2 measurement defect. Original bytes are preserved; the named study authors the native pipeline and aligns actual repeated work.

observation: The two sizes (32,768 and 65,536 keys) exercise the complete eight-digit SDK radix pipeline, including all six kernel stages per digit. Independent Python integer simulation checks every final key, local temporary key, histogram, local start, global prefix, and top-level scan buffer in all 20 captures. The second fixture has 1,024 lower-28-bit groups, every upper nibble in each group, and four copies of each full key. This is stronger than the legacy monotonic-only check, which cannot prove multiset preservation. All three Julia versions retain the pipeline but use an explicit block scan instead of the native warp-synchronous helper. Thus synchronization adaptation is a concrete performance explanation candidate; no bottleneck or occupancy claim is made without counters.
effort_observation: One authored device candidate per model. CUDA.jl has two successful program checks across a fixture-only coverage refinement, not a compiler or numerical repair. KA and JACC each have one successful program/JIT check compiling six authored kernels. Prospective usage windows include verification and metadata, not exclusive billed coding cost.
